L8: # WCVM scientists seeking dogs with spreading cancer for clinical trial
L9: 
L10: Oncology researchers at the Western College of Veterinary Medicine (WCVM) are seeking dogs with spreading cancer for a clinical trial at the WCVM Veterinary Medical Centre.
L11: 
L12: May 20, 2024
L13: #### Deciphering tumour heterogeneity through necropsy, imaging and transcriptomics in naturally occurring cancers in dogs.
L14: 
L15: One out of every four dogs is diagnosed with cancer, and sadly, half of those animals will die of the disease. Cancer's ability to spread is a major challenge, making it difficult to detect and treat effectively.
L16: 
L17: This clinical trial at the WCVM will explore potential solutions by using a new approach to studying cancer spreading in canine patients.
L18: WCVM researchers will study cancer spreading in pet dogs diagnosed with cancer using two tools: positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) imaging, an advanced imaging technology, and RNA sequencing, a gene profiling method.
L19: 
L20: The WCVM is the only Canadian veterinary college equipped with PET-CT technology. The state-of-the-art equipment allows allows human and veterinary cancer researchers at the University of Saskatchewan to offer this unique opportunity to pet owners.

L7: # Radiation oncology trials: canine patients
L8: 
L9: WCVM researchers are seeking canine patients for two radiation oncology trials.
L10: 
L11: Researchers at the Western College of Veterinary Medicine (WCVM) are seeking canine patients for two radiation oncology clinical trials. If you have a dog that may be a potential candidate for these studie, please share this information with your veterinarian or contact Dr. Monique Mayer (monique.mayer@usask.ca) for more information.
L12: 
L13: ###
L14: ### Nasal tumours
L15: 
L16: The objective of this study is to determine if cone-beam computed tomography acquired with a linear accelerator provides comparable radiation treatment planning to a diagnostic CT scan.
L17: 
L18:   * Tumour type: Nasal tumour, any histopathological diagnosis
L19:   * Species: Dog
L20:   * Inclusion: Patient will undergo radiation therapy at the VMC
L21:   * Study pays for: radiation planning CT scan, CT contrast agent
L22:   * Contact: Dr. Monique Mayer (monique.mayer@usask.ca)
L23: ### Oral melanoma
L24: 
L25: Oral melanoma is the most common malignant oral tumour diagnosed in dogs, with a high risk of distant metastasis. The objective of the clinical trial is to determine whether PET-CT (positron emission tomography-computed tomography) technology provides more accurate staging information than computed tomography (CT) alone for dogs with oral melanoma.

L8: # Frequently Asked Questions
L9: 
L10: What is a clinical trial? How do veterinary clinical trials impact human medicine? What would my participation involve? Find out the answers to these questions and more.
L11: 
L12: Typical questions and answers that can help you understand how clinical trials play such a critical role in the development of new treatments for naturally occurring diseases:
L13: ### What is a clinical trial?
L14: 
L15: When a new medical product or clinical approach is being studied, it is helpful to determine whether or not it will be effective in treating a disease or condition, and to what extent. Investigators try to determine this by measuring certain outcomes in the patients that are taking part.
L16: ### How do veterinary clinical trials impact human medicine?
L17: 
L18: Not only does medicine in the veterinary setting benefit the animals we aim to treat, it brings us one step closer to treating humans with comparable diseases.
L19: 
L20: Many diseases that occur in humans are also seen in animals. Our research at the Dick Vet can help to provide information that will can be used in human medicine as the basis for new treatments for similar diseases.
